summary: Defines an experimental extension to IMAP that lets clients and servers store metadata, such as comments or flags, on whole messages or on individual message parts kept in a server mailbox. It was published as Experimental because the working group wanted implementation and deployment experience before moving toward a standards-track version, and it warns that later versions may change incompatibly.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5257 lets a mail server hold notes about the messages it stores. A client can attach a comment to a whole message or to one part of it, such as marking a single attachment as read or important. Each note has a private version that only you see and a shared version that everyone with access to the mailbox can see, so a team can work from the same notes while keeping personal ones to itself.

questions: how to attach comments to email messages on imap server
how to store comments on imap messages
subtitle: How an IMAP server can store comments, flags and other notes on messages and on individual message parts.

tldr.problem: IMAP has no standard way to attach extra information, such as a comment or a note against one part of a message, so each client keeps its own notes locally.
tldr.mechanism: The extension gives every message a set of named entries, each holding attributes such as a value and a size. Every attribute exists in a private version and a shared version, and the extension adds FETCH, STORE, APPEND, SEARCH and SORT support for them.
tldr.outcome: Notes can live on the server and follow a message when it is copied. The document is Experimental and warns that it may change incompatibly before it becomes a standard.

today: RFC 5257 is an Experimental document and has not been obsoleted or updated. The memo says it came out of a working group with good consensus on the approach, but that the group did not have enough information about implementation and deployment hurdles to meet the requirements of a Proposed Standard, and that it solicits implementations and implementation reports. It also warns that the specification may change incompatibly on the way to Proposed Standard, and that any such change will come with a new capability name so that deployments of the experimental extension are not affected.

sections.title: What the ANNOTATE Extension Adds
sections.content:
ANNOTATE is present in any IMAP implementation that lists ANNOTATE-EXPERIMENT-1 among its supported capabilities. It makes ten changes to the base protocol: a new ANNOTATION data item for FETCH, another for STORE, a search criterion, a sort key, a data item for APPEND, a new requirement on COPY, an ANNOTATE parameter for SELECT and EXAMINE, two response codes reporting a failure to store an annotation, and a new access control right for use with the ACL extensions.

The storage model for annotations is based on the Application Configuration Access Protocol in RFC 2244. There is no inheritance between annotations. A server that supports annotations must store all annotation data permanently, so there is no equivalent of the session-only flags in the base IMAP specification. For the best support of a client that needs to synchronise annotations while offline, the memo also recommends support for the Conditional STORE extension.

The memo is explicit about its own status. It says the working group had good consensus on the approach but did not have enough information about implementation and deployment hurdles to meet all the requirements of a Proposed Standard, and that the IETF solicits implementations and implementation reports to make further progress. Implementers are told that the specification may change incompatibly on the way to Proposed Standard, and that any such change will come with a new capability name so that deployments of the experimental extension are not broken.
sections.plainLanguage: The extension adds notes to messages held on a mail server, and it adds the commands needed to read, write, search and sort by those notes. The server keeps them permanently, so a note is still there after the client disconnects.

sections.title: Entries and Attributes
sections.content:
The data model uses a uniquely named entry that holds a set of standard attributes, so a single coherent piece of metadata about a message is one entry made of several attributes. A comment on a message, for example, has the entry name /comment and is made of attributes such as value and size that carry the properties and the data of the entry.

Entry names are hierarchical, with each component separated by a slash, and they must not contain two consecutive slashes or end with one. Attribute names are hierarchical in the same way but separated by a period. The value of an attribute is either NIL, meaning it has no value, or a string of zero or more octets. Entry and attribute names must not contain an asterisk or a percent sign, non-ASCII characters or the NULL octet, and an invalid name produces a BAD response. The names are case-sensitive.

The document registers an initial set of names. The top-level / entry holds nothing itself: entries whose name starts with a digit refer to a body part, and all others refer to the whole message. /comment is a note on the whole message, /altsubject holds a subject supplied by the recipient for the client to use instead of the original, and /flags is reserved for future use. Under a body part there are /comment and a /flags entry whose sub-entries mirror the standard IMAP flags \Seen, \Answered, \Flagged and $Forwarded for that one part, with the value set to 1, 0 or NIL. A /vendor entry lets a product store its own annotations under a registered vendor token. Only two attributes are defined: value, the text or binary data itself, which the client deletes by storing NIL, and size, the length of the value in octets, which the server sets and clients can only read.
sections.plainLanguage: Notes are stored under names. A name is a path, such as /comment for a note on the whole message or /1/comment for a note on the first part. Each name holds one or more attributes, of which only two exist: the value itself and its size.

sections.title: Private and Shared Annotations
sections.content:
Some IMAP mailboxes belong to one user and some are shared. That raises the question of whether an annotation is private or shared. If all annotations were private, a shared mailbox such as a folder of bug reports could never carry notes that the whole team reads, which is a useful thing to want. If all were shared, there would be no way to keep a personal note in a shared mailbox, and granting another user access to a mailbox could unintentionally expose private information. Often both are wanted: an administrator sets shared notes on a message in a shared folder, and individual users add their own on top.

The proposal is two standard suffixes for every attribute, .shared and .priv. A SEARCH or FETCH that names neither uses both. STORE, APPEND and SORT must name one explicitly, so a client can never store an annotation without knowing whether it is shared or private. Where the extension is present, support for shared annotations in servers is required and support for private annotations is optional, because tracking who owns a private annotation, and how much of a user's quota it consumes, adds real complexity. Clients that support the extension must handle both.

Access is governed by rights. Where the ACL extension is present, the server must recognise a new n right. For private values the r right controls both reading and writing. For shared values the r right controls reading and the new n right controls writing, which counts as a shared flag right in RFC 4314. Without the ACL extension, access follows the state of the mailbox: private values can be read in any mailbox that was selected or examined, and written in one selected read-write. The extension does not expose the standard IMAP flags and keywords as entries, because the mapping between shared and private values and the base flags is ambiguous; clients that need shared and private flags are to create their own annotation entries instead.
sections.plainLanguage: Every note exists twice: once for you alone and once for everybody who can see the mailbox. You have to say which one you mean when you write a note, so a private note is never written into a shared slot by accident. The server can also control who may read and who may write shared notes.

sections.title: The New IMAP Commands
sections.content:
SELECT and EXAMINE must return an ANNOTATIONS response code saying what level of support the mailbox has. The code is NONE when the mailbox has no annotation support at all, READ-ONLY when its annotations cannot be changed, NOPRIVATE when only shared annotations are supported, and a number giving the maximum size in octets of an annotation value. Servers must accept annotation values of at least 1024 octets, and must provide at least 10 annotations per message. The ANNOTATE parameter on SELECT and EXAMINE turns on unsolicited notifications; it is a per-mailbox state change, so it must be repeated on every such command to stay in effect.

FETCH gains an ANNOTATION data item that takes an entry specifier and an attribute specifier. The asterisk and the percent sign can be used as wildcards in entry specifiers, where the percent sign matches one level of the hierarchy but not the slash. STORE gains an ANNOTATION data item that sets or replaces attributes, and clients remove an attribute by storing NIL. It behaves as if it had the .SILENT flag, so the server does not send back an untagged FETCH. If a value is too large the server must return a tagged NO with an [ANNOTATE TOOBIG] code, and if the mailbox has reached its limit of annotations it must return a tagged NO with [ANNOTATE TOOMANY].

APPEND can carry annotations for the message being appended, including through the multi-append extension. SEARCH gains an ANNOTATION criterion that looks for a string in the value of an annotation, where only the value, value.priv and value.shared attributes may be searched. SORT gains an ANNOTATION key, where only value.priv and value.shared may be used, and the entry must be given in full because wildcards are not allowed. Servers should send unsolicited annotation notices when a third party changes an entry, but such notices must carry only the entry name and never the value, so that large values are not pushed to a client that did not ask for them.

COPY has a new requirement. For each message copied, the server must copy the private annotation data belonging to the current user and all the shared annotation data, except where the destination mailbox does not allow one kind, does not support annotations, or cannot hold an annotation of that size. Private annotation data belonging to other users must not be copied.
sections.plainLanguage: Notes can be read, written, searched for, sorted by and attached to a message as it is filed. They also travel with a message when it is copied to another mailbox, except for private notes that belong to somebody else.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo makes one point of its own: an annotation whose value is meant to stay private must be stored in a .priv value rather than a .shared one, because shared values may be visible to other users.

Beyond that, the extension raises no security considerations that are not already present in the base IMAP protocol, and those are discussed in RFC 3501. The internationalization rules of the base protocol also apply: servers must follow the standard IMAP text normalisation, character set conversion and collation rules when annotations are searched or sorted, and text values are expected to use UTF-8.
sections.plainLanguage: The only new risk is choosing the wrong kind of note. A note meant to be private has to be stored as private, or others with access to the mailbox can read it. Otherwise the extension is no more dangerous than IMAP itself.
